title: Calculating EU PPWR Article 24 Empty-Space Ratios (<=50%) for E-Commerce Boxes in Pure JavaScript
summary: Under the European Union's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation ( Regulation (EU) 2025/40 , PPWR), Article 24 introduces a 50% maximum empty-space ratio for grouped, transport, and e-commerce mailer packaging—and void fillers such as air pillows, bubble wrap, and crinkle paper count as empty space , not product volume. When building custom packaging configurators or cartonization scripts for DTC brands shipping to Europe, checking internal box volume against clustered SKU geometry upfront prevents non-compliant stock box selection. 1. Bounding-Box & Flute Caliper Clearance Formula Corrugated mailers (such as E-flute ~1.6 mm or B-flute ~3.0 mm) require internal folding clearance beyond raw product dimensions, especially on double-wall roll-end tuck-top (RETT) mailers: export function evaluatePpwrVoidRatio ( productClusterMm , innerBoxMm ) { const productVolMm3 = productClusterMm . l * productClusterMm . w * productClusterMm . h ; const boxVolMm3 = innerBoxMm . l * innerBoxMm . w * innerBoxMm . h ; if ( boxVolMm3 <= 0 || boxVolMm3 < productVolMm3 ) { throw new Error ( 'Inner box dimensions must enclose the product cluster.' ) ; } const emptySpaceRatio = ( ( boxVolMm3 - productVolMm3 ) / boxVolMm3 ) * 100 ; const maxCompliantBoxVolCm3 = ( productVolMm3 / 0.5 ) / 1000 ; return { productVolumeCm3 : Math . round ( productVolMm3 / 1000 ) , innerBoxVolumeCm3 : Math . round ( boxVolMm3 / 1000 ) , emptySpacePct : Number ( emptySpaceRatio . toFixed ( 1 ) ) , compliant : emptySpaceRatio <= 50 , maxAllowedBoxVolumeCm3 : Math . round ( maxCompliantBoxVolCm3 ) } ; } 2. Why Stock Cartons Fail Multi-Item Beauty & Confectionery Kits A common failure pattern in subscription and DTC fulfillment is dropping a 180 × 120 × 65 mm skincare jar cluster ( 1,404 cm³ ) into a standard 260 × 200 × 110 mm ( 5,720 cm³ ) stock corrugated mailer stuffed with paper shreds. Even though the box feels full, its statutory empty-space ratio is 75.5% —well above the 50% threshold. Right-sizing to a 200 × 140 × 80 mm ( 2,240 cm³ ) custom E-flute mailer brings the empty-space ratio down to 37.3% while cutting dimensional freight weight. 3. title: Today in AI: a claimed 9/4 matrix multiplication result, a shorter Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and a code golf record
summary: Three AI stories from the last 48 hours that are worth a builder's attention. 1. OpenAI claims the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4 Per Scott Aaronson's write-up, OpenAI says it proved the exponent omega equals 9/4, with the lower bound matching the known upper bound. If it holds up, it closes a question researchers have chased for decades. It still needs independent review. 2. Anthropic posts a much shorter Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis Luke Sernau and colleagues cut the machine-checked proof from about 300k lines to about 76k. It is verified by software, but no mathematician has read it end to end yet. The thing to scrutinize is whether the formal definitions say what we actually mean, because Lean only checks the proof against the statement as written. 3. GPT-6.2 Astra beats the 2015 Google code golfers A new benchmark has it scoring about 92% on JS, Python and C++, ahead of the 2015 human results. Code golf rewards search and experimentation, not only recall, which is why it is a decent signal for agentic work. The comment threads also show people debating whether the model regressed on chat and writing. The pattern Models are getting spiky: superhuman where a cheap verifier exists, flatter elsewhere. That makes verification, not generation, the bottleneck. Which of these is actually changing how you work? Curious where you land.

title: A popularity table of my skills opens with the last step
summary: He asked for a list of his agents' most popular skills, then decided the first 20 rows should be tasks, not a ranking. The fleet counter backs the decision: 277 skills on the shelf, 3,354 calls since June, the top 20 take 71% of all calls - and #1 is the end-of-session retro at 31%. A popularity table opens with the last thing you do, not the first 1. ⭐⭐⭐ The ranking he asked for, measured. Fleet skill-usage counter, _machine-bus/_metrics/skill-usage/*.jsonl , 5 writer nodes, n= 3,354 calls, 2026-06-06 → 2026-11-24, 182 distinct names. Top of the list: retro 1,050 (31.3%) · dr-fanout 150 · claudeai-sync 129 · alpha-judge 128 · tt 106 · voice-sessions 97 · alfa-search-recall-deepresearch 94 · intake 65 · intention 58 · coach 56. Top 20 = 70.7% of all calls. 2. ⭐⭐⭐ Why a popularity list fails a newcomer. Row 1 is the retrospective that closes a session. Rows 3, 4 and 6 are mostly background work: syncing old web chats, a judge for mined candidates, voice notes turned into sessions. Rows 2 and 7 are deep-research rituals. Someone arriving with "I need to answer a lead" or "my machines stopped syncing" finds neither verb in the first ten rows. The list answers "what runs most", and the question was "where do I start". 3. ⭐⭐ The long tail is almost half the shelf. On this node 277 skills have a SKILL.md . 160 were called at least once anywhere in the fleet; 117 (42%) never. 66 names were called once or twice. A table sorted by calls would bury nearly half the shelf below row 160, including runbooks that are supposed to sit at zero until the day they are needed ( runbook_skills.txt lists 27 of them, e.g. raise-sync , reboot ). 4. ⭐⭐ The ranking also splits one tool in two. systematic-debugging 41 + superpowers:systematic-debugging 40 : the same skill under two names, each landing around rows 18-19. Merged, it is 81 calls and row 9. A popularity table built straight from the counter would show it twice and rank it too low. 5. ⭐⭐ The counter itself has been half-blind since October. Last write per node: hub 2026-10-02 · ZBOOK 2026-10-02 · MacBook 2026-10-01 · anchor 2026-08-18 · this node 2026-11-24 . For the last ~55 days only one machine reports. The ranking above describes June-September work, not this month. 6. What the task-first table needs that the counter cannot give. Skill descriptions are written for the router, not for the reader: median 338 characters, 14 over the 400-character limit. A task row needs a short human verb ("answer a lead", "the sync is down", "prepare for a call") and one arrow to one skill. That mapping is editorial work - the counter can only tell which rows deserve a place in the top 20. 7. ⚠️ Limits. Counts are invocations logged by a hook, not completed work; routine-triggered calls ( origin:unknown , 40+ of them) are mixed with human ones. Shelf numbers are this node's receive-only copy. Five nodes' logs travel over a bus that has been silent since early October. 📖 Longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261125.md 🤖 Devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261125.md 🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI Invented by Mycroft and Tony Dzi (Anton Dziatkovskii), Palo Alto AI Research Lab. title: Teaching AI About Disordered Proteins? I’d Start at 50 Milliseconds
summary: If AlphaFold gives you 25 different pictures of two proteins bound together, which one would you trust enough to plan an experiment around? A LinkedIn post about AlphaFold and disordered proteins got me thinking about that question from the lab’s side. I think there’s a specific gap we can fill with FastHDX. We can measure which stretches of a disordered protein change when a partner binds, including changes that are visible only in the first fraction of a second of labelling. Put those measurements in a public databank and the same experiment can help one team judge a structure today and another train a model to predict which regions will respond in the next protein pair. One team really did have 25 models to choose from In a study of the progesterone receptor and its partner SRC3 , Matthew Mann and colleagues generated 25 AlphaFold 3 models. Both proteins have large disordered regions. Across predictions, one of the things that varied most was where the two proteins sat relative to each other. The researchers used hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and a program called HDXer to identify the model that best fit their measurements for visualization. You can download the experimental data from PRIDE under PXD056400 . An intrinsically disordered protein (IDP), or an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) within a larger protein, can sample many shapes. Some regions settle into a fold when they bind. Others stay mobile even with a partner attached. In a benchmark of known complexes , AlphaFold-Multimer produced at least acceptable structures for more than 76% of cases in each dataset. For the group that stayed particularly flexible when bound, only about 3% of predictions reached the high-quality category. That’s a good reason to use the software and an equally good reason to ask what the protein actually did in solution. What FastHDX can capture before two samples look the same In HDX-MS, a lab exposes the protein to heavy water. Hydrogens along its backbone exchange with deuterium. After a set time, the lab slows the exchange, cuts the protein into short pieces called peptides, and measures how much deuterium each peptide picked up. Run the protein alone and again with its partner already bound. A peptide that takes up less deuterium in the complex has become more protected. The partner might touch that stretch directly, or binding elsewhere might stabilize it. The progesterone receptor study’s first labelled sample was at 10 seconds . Why would I want to start earlier? Consider a domain of CREB-binding protein. In an early experiment, exchange was nearly complete across the free domain by ten seconds . When researchers measured the same region on a millisecond timescale , they could distinguish its fast-exchanging ends from its slower centre. Adding its binding partner, ACTR, protected the centre further. A ten-second reading alone could miss what made those regions different. Nicoya specifies a labelling range of 50 milliseconds to 24 hours for FastHDX . It automates the mixing and quenching upstream of the mass spectrometer. That means I can put the free protein and the complex on the same schedule, early enough to catch fast exchange and long enough to follow the protected stretches. Here, 50 milliseconds is the time the sample spends in heavy water. The partners have already had time to bind. There’s a disordered protein example from the instrument’s own history. Neeleema Seetaloo and colleagues studied full-length, monomeric α-synuclein on the FastHDX prototype called ms2min . Across the solution conditions they tested, faster exchange around residues 115–135 correlated with a shorter wait for aggregation to begin. The sequence was identical every time. The exchange curves and the buffer tell a model something the sequence alone can’t. Where the data go, and who already uses them The developers of HDXRank collected experimental HDX data from PRIDE and MassIVE , trained a model to rank candidate structures of protein complexes, and released their training dataset . For training and evaluation, they chose 30 seconds to 10 minutes because that interval contained the most uptake measurements. That’s where I see an opening for labs with FastHDX. We can contribute paired measurements in the first second, while some of the most flexible peptides are still picking up label. What we can share Where another team can find it Raw spectra, peptide uptake tables and experimental conditions Deposit them together in PRIDE or MassIVE . For a real example, a study of engineered protein switches used ms2min from 100 milliseconds to 100 seconds and deposited its HDX data as PXD073666 . Published experimental evidence that a particular sequence region is disordered Submit the evidence to DisProt for curation. Its α-synuclein entry shows how readers can trace a regional annotation back to an experiment. A set of three-dimensional conformations built or refined using the data Deposit the ensemble in the Protein Ensemble Database and link it to the experimental dataset so researchers can examine both. What I’d actually give a model developer Suppose one peptide takes up 3.0 daltons alone and 1.8 with its partner at 250 milliseconds . By ten seconds, both samples reach 5.0. Those numbers are hypothetical. Here’s how I’d use them. Give the model the two sequences, the peptide’s position, the solution conditions and the labelling time. Ask it to predict the change in uptake. The measured answer is −1.2 daltons at 250 milliseconds and zero at ten seconds . A peptide the lab never detected gets marked as missing. That ten-second zero is worth keeping. For a pilot, I’d measure one known pair at 50 ms, 250 ms, 1 s, 10 s and 1 minute. Two states and three independent repeats make 30 timed measurements. At Nicoya’s stated 8 µL per time point , that’s 240 µL for the timed measurements , before controls and handling losses. The autosampler lets a lab queue additional pairs on that same schedule. I’d publish one row per peptide, state, time and replicate, with the raw file reference, sequences, concentrations, pH, temperature and deuterium fraction, following the HDX-MS reporting recommendations . Once enough families are represented, I’d hold one entire protein family back from training. Give two models the same measurement budget, let one learn from early and late data and the other from later times alone, then ask each to rank the held-out peptides by how much binding protects them. The useful result for a lab is whether those first few time points change which stretch it would investigate next. That’s why I’d choose FastHDX to help build this dataset. We can always take another model back to an archived spectrum. We can’t take a ten-second sample back to 250 milliseconds to recover a difference that’s already gone. If we want AI to get better at disordered proteins, I’d start by making those first 50 milliseconds as easy to download as a predicted structure. title: Design a Trustworthy Vehicle Maintenance Timeline in Python
summary: A car-history app looks simple until two data sources disagree. One workshop reports a brake service at 62,000 kilometers. An inspection center records 61,500 kilometers a week later. Another provider sends the same service record twice, using slightly different timestamps. If the application merely sorts those rows by date, the result may look convincing while quietly misleading the reader. The hard part is not drawing the timeline. It is designing a trustworthy event pipeline behind it. In this tutorial, we'll build a small Python prototype for receiving vehicle maintenance events, normalizing them, detecting duplicates, and surfacing inconsistencies without pretending that the software knows which source is correct. Start with events, not a single vehicle record A typical early design stores one mutable object per vehicle: { "vehicle_id": "demo-42", "last_service": "2026-10-02", "odometer_km": 62000 } This is convenient for a dashboard, but it loses the questions that matter: Who provided the reading? When did the service actually happen? When did the system receive it? Was an earlier reading overwritten? Instead, represent each observation as an event. A derived vehicle summary can still exist, but the source events remain available for inspection. { "event_id": "workshop-A:invoice-781", "vehicle_id": "demo-42", "event_type": "service", "occurred_at": "2026-10-02T09:30:00+03:30", "received_at": "2026-10-03T08:15:00Z", "odometer_km": 62000, "source": "workshop-A" } The two timestamps serve different purposes. occurred_at describes the claimed real-world event. received_at describes when the application learned about it. Keeping both makes delayed imports and backdated corrections easier to investigate. Define a small, explicit validation boundary The following code uses only Python's standard library. It intentionally handles a narrow event schema rather than trying to anticipate every workshop, insurer, or inspection system. from datetime import datetime, timezone ALLOWED_TYPES = {"service", "inspection", "repair", "odometer"} def to_utc(value: str) -> datetime: parsed = datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00")) if parsed.tzinfo is None: raise ValueError("Timestamp must include a UTC offset") return parsed.astimezone(timezone.utc) def normalize_event(raw: dict) -> dict: required = { "event_id", "vehicle_id", "event_type", "occurred_at", "received_at", "odometer_km", "source" } missing = required - raw.keys() if missing: raise ValueError(f"Missing fields: {sorted(missing)}") if raw["event_type"] not in ALLOWED_TYPES: raise ValueError("Unknown event type") if not all(isinstance(raw[key], str) and raw[key].strip() for key in ("event_id", "vehicle_id", "source")): raise ValueError("Identifiers and source must be nonempty strings") reading = raw["odometer_km"] if reading is not None and (type(reading) is not int or reading < 0): raise ValueError("odometer_km must be a nonnegative integer or null") return { "event_id": raw["event_id"], "vehicle_id": raw["vehicle_id"], "event_type": raw["event_type"], "occurred_at": to_utc(raw["occurred_at"]), "received_at": to_utc(raw["received_at"]), "odometer_km": reading, "source": raw["source"], } Requiring an explicit time-zone offset avoids treating a local wall-clock time as if it were already UTC. Requiring an integer odometer reading also prevents ambiguous text such as "about 62k" from entering calculations unnoticed. That original text may still be useful, but it belongs in a separate raw-data record. For a production system, schema evolution, access controls, a durable event store, and country-specific vehicle identifiers would need separate decisions. Make repeated deliveries safe Imports are retried. Webhooks are delivered more than once. A user can upload the same file twice. These are ordinary operational events, not exceptional failures. An event_id should therefore identify a source event consistently. A database can enforce uniqueness on a combination such as (source, event_id). In a small prototype, we can illustrate the rule with a set: seen = set() accepted = [] def receive(raw: dict) -> str: event = normalize_event(raw) key = (event["source"], event["event_id"]) if key in seen: return "duplicate" seen.add(key) accepted.append(event) return "accepted" The uniqueness check and insertion must be atomic in a real database. Otherwise, two workers could simultaneously accept the same event. A repeated identifier with changed content also deserves investigation rather than a silent overwrite; retain the raw payload or a content fingerprint for comparison. Flag impossible-looking sequences without rewriting history Suppose the sorted readings for one vehicle are 48,000 km, 62,000 km, and then 61,500 km. A consumer-facing interface should not silently replace the last number with 62,000. Nor should it automatically label the lower reading fraudulent. A transcription error, replaced instrument cluster, or source-matching mistake may explain it. The safer behavior is to create a review flag: def odometer_flags(events: list[dict]) -> list[dict]: readings = sorted( (e for e in events if e["odometer_km"] is not None), key=lambda e: (e["occurred_at"], e["event_id"]), ) flags = [] for previous, current in zip(readings, readings[1:]): if current["odometer_km"] < previous["odometer_km"]: flags.append({ "type": "reading_decreased", "previous_event": previous["event_id"], "current_event": current["event_id"], }) return flags This is a consistency check, not a fraud detector. For a multi-source feed, two readings may even describe different points within the same day, with uncertain event times. A production pipeline should preserve that uncertainty instead of manufacturing precision. Other useful flags include unusually large jumps over short periods, a received timestamp far earlier than the claimed occurrence, repeated invoices with different identifiers, and mismatched vehicle identifiers. Each flag needs a documented interpretation and an escalation path. Keep provenance visible in the API An API returning only a polished timeline hides the very information readers might need to assess it. Consider returning the event and its context together: { "vehicle_id": "demo-42", "events": [ { "event_id": "workshop-A:invoice-781", "event_type": "service", "odometer_km": 62000, "source": "workshop-A", "status": "reported" } ], "review_flags": ["reading_decreased"] } A status such as reported means the application received a claim. It does not mean the claim was independently verified. If verification is performed, record who verified it, by which process, and when. Do not collapse these states into an unexplained green checkmark. For broader Persian-language discussion of vehicles, automotive technology, and the car ecosystem, Automadar provides an automotive-focused publication. The engineering lesson here is narrower: a maintenance timeline earns trust by showing where its records came from. Privacy is part of the data model Vehicle history can reveal more than a repair. Timestamps and workshop locations may expose movement patterns; owner contact details may be included in imported documents. Decide what the timeline actually needs before ingesting entire invoices. Separate identifiers used for matching from personally identifiable information. Avoid displaying raw workshop notes to other users. Define retention and correction workflows, and require authorization before exposing detailed vehicle records. If the application supports users in multiple jurisdictions, review the relevant privacy and consumer-disclosure requirements rather than assuming a single policy fits every market. Test the failure modes, not just the happy path Before releasing even a prototype, verify these cases: The same (source, event_id) arrives twice. Two sources reuse the same event ID for unrelated events. A timestamp has no time-zone offset. odometer_km is negative, a string, or a Boolean value. A late-arriving event belongs chronologically between two existing events. A corrected reading conflicts with a previously published summary. A vehicle identifier is missing or maps to more than one record. Tests should assert not only that bad data is rejected or flagged but also that no valid historical event is silently lost. The larger design lesson A vehicle-history interface is a projection of an evidence trail. Good dashboards are useful, but they cannot restore provenance that was discarded upstream. Capture claims as immutable events, keep arrival time separate from occurrence time, prevent accidental duplication, and present anomalies as reviewable facts rather than automatic verdicts. The result is a modest system that is easier to audit, correct, and extend—exactly the properties a real automotive data product needs. Disclosure: This tutorial was prepared with AI assistance. Its prototype code illustrates data-validation principles and is not a production-ready vehicle-history system.

title: Paystack + Next.js: Payments You Can Actually Trust
summary: --- title: "Paystack + Next.js: Payments You Can Actually Trust" published: false date: 2026-11-26 08:00:00 UTC tags: Paystack,Nextjs,Payments,Security canonical_url: https://oyeleke.com.ng/blog/paystack-nextjs-integration Getting a Paystack checkout to open takes ten minutes. Getting it to be correct — every successful payment fulfilled exactly once, no fake confirmations, no orders stuck on "pending" because someone closed the tab — takes a bit more thought. This is the pattern I use for Paystack in Next.js App Router projects, including online giving on the NWPM church platform . It has four parts: Initialize the transaction on the server, with a price the server decides. Complete it on Paystack's checkout. Verify it on the server before delivering anything. Listen for webhooks, so payments are fulfilled even when the browser never comes back. The one rule The browser can start a payment. Only your server, talking to Paystack, can decide that a payment happened . Everything below follows from that. Never trust an amount the browser sends you, and never treat "the user landed on my success page" as proof of payment. Paystack's own docs say the same: visiting the callback URL doesn't prove the transaction succeeded. Setup Get your secret key from the Paystack dashboard ( Settings → API Keys & Webhooks ) and generate a webhook signing secret under Developers → API configuration . Use test keys locally. # .env.local PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY = sk_test_xxx # server only, never NEXT_PUBLIC_ PAYSTACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET = whsec_xxx # webhook signing secret NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL = http : //localhost:3000 1. A tiny server-only Paystack client // lib/paystack.ts import "server-only" ; const API = "https://api.paystack.co" ; async function paystack < T > ( path : string , init ?: RequestInit ) : Promise < T > { const res = await fetch ( `${API}${path}` , { . . . init , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${process.env.PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY}` , "Content-Type" : "application/json" , . . . init ? . headers , } , cache : "no-store" , } ) ; const body = await res . json ( ) ; if ( ! res . ok || ! body . status ) throw new Error ( body . message ?? `Paystack error ${res.status}` ) ; return body . data as T ; } export function initializeTransaction ( input : { email : string ; amount : number ; // in kobo (the currency's subunit) reference : string ; callback_url : string ; metadata ?: Record < string , unknown > ; } ) { return paystack < { authorization_url : string ; access_code : string ; reference : string } > ( "/transaction/initialize" , { method : "POST" , body : JSON . stringify ( input ) } , ) ; } export function verifyTransaction ( reference : string ) { return paystack < { status : string ; amount : number ; currency : string ; reference : string } > ( `/transaction/verify/${encodeURIComponent(reference)}` , ) ; } The server-only import makes the build fail if this file is ever pulled into a client component, which is exactly what you want for anything holding your secret key. 2. Initialize on the server, with your price The client sends what it wants to buy. The server decides how much it costs, creates a pending order, and asks Paystack for a checkout URL. // app/api/checkout/route.ts import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto" ; import { initializeTransaction } from "@/lib/paystack" ; import { db } from "@/lib/db" ; // your database client export async function POST ( req : Request ) { const { productId , email } = await req . json ( ) ; const product = await db . product . findUnique ( { where : { id : productId } } ) ; if ( ! product ) return Response . json ( { error : "Unknown product" } , { status : 400 } ) ; const reference = randomUUID ( ) ; await db . order . create ( { data : { reference , productId , email , amountKobo : product . priceKobo , currency : "NGN" , status : "pending" } , } ) ; const { authorization_url } = await initializeTransaction ( { email , amount : product . priceKobo , // ₦5,000 → 500000 reference , callback_url : `${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL}/checkout/complete` , metadata : { productId } , } ) ; return Response . json ( { url : authorization_url } ) ; } Two details that matter: Amounts are in the subunit. ₦5,000 is 500000 kobo. Store prices in kobo as integers everywhere and you'll never fight floating-point rounding. You own the reference. Generate it yourself and save it before calling Paystack. That reference is how every later step — verification, webhooks, retries — finds the order. 3. Send the customer to Paystack's checkout The simplest flow that works everywhere, including flaky mobile browsers, is a redirect. Return the authorization_url from your route and send the customer there. When they finish, Paystack redirects them to your callback_url with the transaction reference in the query string. The route in step 2 already returns that URL. The button just follows it: // components/PayButton.tsx "use client" ; import { useState } from "react" ; export function PayButton ( { productId , email } : { productId : string ; email : string } ) { const [ loading , setLoading ] = useState ( false ) ; async function pay ( ) { setLoading ( true ) ; const res = await fetch ( "/api/checkout" , { method : "POST" , headers : { "Content-Type" : "application/json" } , body : JSON . stringify ( { productId , email } ) , } ) ; if ( ! res . ok ) return setLoading ( false ) ; const { url } = await res . json ( ) ; window . location . assign ( url ) ; } return ( < button onClick = { pay } disabled = { loading } > { loading ? "Opening checkout…" : "Pay with Paystack" } </ button > ) ; } Prefer an in-page popup? Return the access_code instead and open it with Paystack's InlineJS library ( npm i @paystack/inline-js ): new Paystack().resumeTransaction(accessCode) . The server-side parts below stay exactly the same. Whichever you choose, the browser finishing checkout only means "the customer says they paid". It doesn't mark anything as paid. 4. Fulfil once, from anywhere Both the completion page and the webhook will call the same function. It verifies with Paystack, checks the amount and currency against your order, and flips the order from pending to paid exactly once. // lib/orders.ts import "server-only" ; import { db } from "@/lib/db" ; import { verifyTransaction } from "@/lib/paystack" ; export async function fulfilOrder ( reference : string ) { const order = await db . order . findUnique ( { where : { reference } } ) ; if ( ! order ) return null ; if ( order . status === "paid" ) return order ; // already done const tx = await verifyTransaction ( reference ) ; const valid = tx . status === "success" && tx . amount === order . amountKobo && tx . currency === order . currency ; if ( ! valid ) return order ; // Conditional update: only one caller can win the pending → paid transition. const { count } = await db . order . updateMany ( { where : { reference , status : "pending" } , data : { status : "paid" , paidAt : new Date ( ) } , } ) ; if ( count === 1 ) { await sendReceipt ( order ) ; // deliver value exactly once } return { . . . order , status : "paid" as const } ; } Why so careful? Check the amount. Paystack explicitly recommends it: if the amount doesn't match what you're delivering, don't deliver. Make it idempotent. The callback page and the webhook will often arrive at nearly the same moment, and Paystack retries webhooks and lets you resend events. Without the conditional pending → paid update, you'll send two receipts or ship two orders. The completion page just calls it: // app/checkout/complete/page.tsx import { fulfilOrder } from "@/lib/orders" ; export default async function CheckoutComplete ( { searchParams , } : { searchParams : Promise < { reference ?: string ; trxref ?: string } > ; } ) { const { reference , trxref } = await searchParams ; const order = await fulfilOrder ( reference ?? trxref ?? "" ) ; if ( order ? . status === "paid" ) return < h1 > Payment received — thank you !</ h1 > ; return < h1 > We & apos ; re confirming your payment . You & apos ; ll get an email shortly . </ h1 > ; } The "still confirming" state isn't a failure. If verification hasn't settled yet, the webhook will finish the job. 5. Webhooks: the part most integrations skip Users close tabs, lose network on the bus, or their phone dies right after paying. The callback page never loads — but Paystack still sends a charge.success event to your webhook URL. This is what makes your integration reliable. Paystack now signs events with a Paystack-Signature header, using a webhook signing secret ( whsec_… ) you generate in the dashboard. It looks like this: Paystack-Signature: t = 1760270400 , v1 = whk_3f9a1c2e : 9d1b . . . e47a To verify it, per Paystack's docs: Read the raw body bytes before any JSON parsing. Take t and every v1 value ( <key id>:<signature> ). Reject events where t is more than 300 seconds from your server's time (replay protection). Compute HMAC-SHA512 of ${t}. + raw body, keyed with the whole whsec_… secret. Compare against each v1 signature in constant time. // lib/paystack-webhook.ts import "server-only" ; import { createHmac , timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto" ; const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300 ; export function verifyPaystackSignature ( raw : Buffer , header : string | null , secret : string ) : boolean { if ( ! header ) return false ; let t : number | null = null ; const signatures : string [ ] = [ ] ; for ( const part of header . split ( "," ) ) { const i = part . indexOf ( "=" ) ; if ( i === - 1 ) continue ; const key = part . slice ( 0 , i ) . trim ( ) ; const value = part . slice ( i + 1 ) . trim ( ) ; if ( key === "t" && /^ \ d + $ / . test ( value ) ) t = Number ( value ) ; if ( key === "v1" ) { const j = value . indexOf ( ":" ) ; if ( j !== - 1 ) signatures . push ( value . slice ( j + 1 ) ) ; } } if ( t === null || signatures . length === 0 ) return false ; if ( Math . abs ( Date . now ( ) / 1000 - t ) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS ) return false ; const expected = createHmac ( "sha512" , secret ) . update ( `${t}.` ) . update ( raw ) . digest ( ) ; return signatures . some ( ( hex ) => /^ [ 0 - 9a - f ] { 128 } $ / . test ( hex ) && timingSafeEqual ( expected , Buffer . from ( hex , "hex" ) ) ) ; } And the route handler. In the App Router you get the raw body with req.arrayBuffer() ; don't call req.json() first, because re-serialising parsed JSON changes the bytes and the signature will never match. // app/api/paystack/webhook/route.ts import { after } from "next/server" ; import { fulfilOrder } from "@/lib/orders" ; import { verifyPaystackSignature } from "@/lib/paystack-webhook" ; export async function POST ( req : Request ) { const raw = Buffer . from ( await req . arrayBuffer ( ) ) ; const secret = process . env . PAYSTACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET ; if ( ! secret ) return new Response ( "Webhook secret not configured" , { status : 500 } ) ; if ( ! verifyPaystackSignature ( raw , req . headers . get ( "paystack-signature" ) , secret ) ) { return new Response ( "Invalid signature" , { status : 401 } ) ; } const event = JSON . parse ( raw . toString ( "utf8" ) ) ; if ( event . event === "charge.success" ) { // Acknowledge fast; do the work after the response is sent. after ( ( ) => fulfilOrder ( event . data . reference ) ) ; } return new Response ( null , { status : 200 } ) ; } A few production notes: Return 200 quickly. Paystack retries anything that isn't a 200 OK — in live mode every 3 minutes for the first 4 tries, then hourly for 72 hours. Long work belongs after the response, which is what after() is for. Return 200 for events you don't handle , too. Otherwise Paystack keeps retrying them. Still verify inside fulfilOrder . The signature proves the event came from Paystack; the verify call and amount check prove it matches your order. Older integrations may only receive the legacy x-paystack-signature header (HMAC-SHA512 of the raw body using your secret key, no timestamp). Paystack's advice is to keep verifying it until your events carry Paystack-Signature , and not to delete your secret key before then. Testing it locally Webhooks can't reach localhost . Expose your dev server with a tunnel (or the Paystack CLI), put that URL in the test webhook field in your dashboard, and make a payment with Paystack's test cards. Then deliberately close the tab right after paying: the order should still end up paid , by webhook. That one test catches most broken integrations. The checklist Secret key and webhook secret are server-only (no NEXT_PUBLIC_ ) Prices come from your database, in kobo, never from the client You generate and store the reference before initializing Every fulfilment path verifies status, amount and currency pending → paid happens in one conditional update (idempotent) Webhook verifies the signature on the raw body and returns 200 fast Tested: pay, then close the tab — order still fulfilled Payments are the one feature where "mostly works" means someone lost money. If you'd like a Paystack integration built or reviewed, that's one of the things I do — or just get in touch . Sources: Paystack: Accept Payments · Paystack: Webhooks · Paystack: Verify Payments

title: Introducing BenchSaaS: Can LLMs Actually Deliver Inside Enterprise Software?
summary: Why "Done!" in a chat window isn't enough — and what 8,850 live runs across CRM, inventory, and finance reveal about today's leading AI models. Most LLM benchmarks test how well a model writes isolated code, solves competition math, or answers multiple-choice trivia. Those evaluations are useful, but they miss the question every CIO, product leader, and enterprise architect actually cares about: When you put an AI model inside live business software, can it finish real operational work without silently corrupting your database? To answer that question with evidence rather than demos, the Nocoly & Mingdao AI Tech Group built BenchSaaS V1.0 — an enterprise application LLM benchmark grounded in real CRM, inventory, procurement, and finance workflows. Built on Live Enterprise Software, Not Toy Mocks BenchSaaS runs on an isomorphic testbed built on Nocoly HAP (Hyper Application Platform) . Instead of synthetic single-API stubs, models operate inside two interconnected business applications — Procurement & Sales (32 tables) and Finance Management (8 tables) — totaling 40 structured business tables and 18,014 real-world business records , complete with relational links, workflow constraints, and audit logs. For the V1.0 evaluation (conducted October 22 – November 19, 2026), BenchSaaS evaluated: 100 real-world enterprise tasks sampled from a 500-task pool across Inventory & Procurement (52) , Finance & Accounting (27) , CRM (20) , and Cross-App tracing (1) — split between 60 read-only lookup/analysis tasks and 40 write or refusal tasks (16 record creations, 20 updates, and 4 refusal/no-change scenarios). 10 leading LLMs across 3 reasoning tiers ( Low , Mid , and High ), producing 30 distinct model configurations . 9,000 planned runs (3 repeats per task per configuration), yielding 8,850 valid runs ( 7,987 PASS , 863 FAIL , with 150 INVALID infrastructure runs tracked separately). Realistic execution guardrails: every run operated under hard limits of 31 turns, 30 tool calls, and a 1,800-second timeout, with automated database restoration between write runs. The Two-Gate Verification That Catches "Polite Failures" Anyone who has piloted AI agents in ERP or CRM workflows knows the most dangerous failure mode isn't a crash — it's a confident, well-written reply claiming a task is finished when the underlying record is broken. BenchSaaS enforces two mandatory verification gates : Gate 1 ( ANSWER_MATCH ): Evaluates the model's written response across all 100 tasks for factual accuracy, calculation correctness, citations, and mandatory write receipts. Gate 2 ( RESULT_CONSISTENCY ): On write tasks, reads back the frozen HAP database snapshot after execution — combining programmatic checks with an independent judge — to verify that every required field, status option, and cross-table relation was actually persisted and matches the model's claim. The results proved why backend verification is non-negotiable: 100% of the 165 Gate-2 database failures in BenchSaaS V1.0 had already passed Gate 1. In every single one of those 165 failures, the model's chat response sounded complete and trustworthy — yet the database snapshot revealed NULL fields, wrong entity codes written into the wrong columns, empty status arrays ( [] ), or values contradicting the model's own summary. In one representative Inventory task (Case 7.4: creating a draft purchase requisition), a model passed Gate 1 and created both the requisition header and line item — yet Gate 2 caught that the mandatory "Available Stock" field had been stored as NULL instead of 20 . Across all 30 configurations, only 44.32% of valid runs passed that task cleanly. Five Takeaways From 8,850 Live Enterprise Runs 1. Strong overall capability — and "Mid" reasoning often beats "High" Across all 8,850 valid runs, models achieved an aggregate solve rate of 90.25% . The top five configurations overall were: #1 Gemini 3.8 Flash (Mid): 97.94% (285/291) · 95.74% 3-of-3 repeat consistency · CNY ¥0.5476/run #2 Gemini 3.8 Flash (High): 97.24% (282/290) · CNY ¥0.7519/run #3 Kimi K3.1 Pro (High): 96.99% (290/299 — highest raw pass count out of 300 planned runs) · CNY ¥0.9273/run #4 DeepSeek V4 Pro (Mid): 96.96% (287/296) · CNY ¥0.9430/run #5 DeepSeek V4 Pro (Low): 96.25% (282/293) · CNY ¥0.8756/run (As the report notes, narrow rank margins should not be over-interpreted given small differences in valid run counts across configurations.) Crucially, turning reasoning effort all the way up did not reliably improve results. While GPT-6-Luna (73.13% → 92.23%), GLM-5.3 (81.82% → 94.54%), and Kimi K3.1 Pro (88.22% → 96.99%) gained significantly at higher tiers, Gemini 3.8 Flash , DeepSeek V4 Pro , and Qwen 3.8 Max all peaked at Mid , and MiniMax M3.1 Flash actually declined at High (79.79% → 76.41%). 2. No single model wins every business domain Enterprise accuracy varies sharply by domain — and different models lead different departments: CRM (95.31% average): Six configurations achieved a 100.00% solve rate ( Kimi K3.1 Pro High , Qwen 3.8 Max Mid , GPT-6-Luna High & Mid , and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Low & High ). Inventory & Procurement (90.02% average): Led by GPT-6.1-Terra (Low) at 98.72% (154/156), narrowly ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) (98.08%) and (Mid) (98.04%). Finance & Accounting (86.56% average — the toughest domain): Led by DeepSeek V4 Pro (Low) at 100.00% (76/76), followed by DeepSeek V4 Pro (Mid) (98.75%) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Mid) (98.67%). 3. Document creation exposes a ~20-point capability cliff Break the 100 tasks down by operational type, and a clear divide emerges. Models excelled at Workflow Tracing (95.35%) , Data Maintenance (95.19%) , and Audit & Reconciliation (95.12%) , and performed solidly on Decision Support (92.29%) , Data Aggregation (88.71%) , and Record Retrieval (84.89%) . Then came Document Creation , where the aggregate solve rate plunged to 76.99% . Creating a multi-table business document — a valid header, complete line items, correct relational links, and compliant status fields — remains the single sharpest differentiator in enterprise AI delivery ( Gemini 3.8 Flash swept the top three spots in Document Creation at 98.2%, 96.4%, and 96.4%). 4. Enterprise failures follow predictable engineering patterns Analyzing all 863 failed runs revealed four dominant root causes: Required Assertion Failures (68.71%, 593 runs): 428 Gate-1 answer gaps and 165 Gate-2 database integrity failures. Business Rule Rejections (18.66%, 161 runs): Attempting to write disallowed or read-only fields, or passing shorthand worksheet aliases instead of valid 24-character table IDs. Invalid Tool Arguments (5.91%, 51 runs): Failing schema validation twice in a row without self-correcting. Tool Budget Exhaustion (5.21%, 45 runs): Hitting the 30-call cap — and notably, 86.7% (39/45) of these runs had zero tool errors, simply burning their budget on brute-force pagination or repetitive lookups. 5. A 134× cost spread makes accuracy-only leaderboards obsolete Across all valid runs, median task latency was 86.55 seconds (ranging from 48.75s for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · Low to 198.01s for Qwen 3.8 Max · High ), while mean cost per run was CNY ¥0.7111 — spanning 134× from ¥0.0241 ( GPT-6-Luna · Low , 73.13%) to ¥3.2358 ( Claude Sonnet 5.5 · High , 92.00%). That spread opens up compelling production tiers depending on your workload: Highest accuracy & repeat stability: Gemini 3.8 Flash · Mid (97.94% solve rate, 95.74% 3-of-3 repeat consistency, ¥0.5476/run). 90%+ high-efficiency value picks: GPT-6-Luna · Mid (90.97% at just ¥0.0302/run ) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · Mid (92.23% at ¥0.1003/run and 57.03s median latency). Fastest 90%+ execution: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · Low (90.91% in 48.75s median at ¥0.0809/run). What This Means for Teams Deploying Enterprise AI If you are building or adopting AI agents inside operational systems, BenchSaaS V1.0 points to three immediate design rules: Never trust verbal completion. Pair every write-capable agent with programmatic post-write verification against actual database state. Route by workflow, not hype. Domain leaders diverge across CRM, inventory, and finance, and "Mid" reasoning frequently outperforms "High" while running faster and cheaper. Evaluate the full delivery triangle. Accuracy alone is misleading without 3-of-3 repeat stability, latency, and per-task unit economics. Explore the Interactive Leaderboard & Full 51-Page Report BenchSaaS V1.0 is live now. You can filter the interactive leaderboard by domain, task type, reasoning tier, latency, and cost on the BenchSaaS V1.0 Landing Page , or download the complete 51-Page English Benchmark Report (PDF) for free. title: How to add an MCP server to Codex (config.toml and codex mcp add)
summary: How to add an MCP server to Codex Checked against the official docs: Oct 27, 2026 Codex (the CLI, the IDE extension and the desktop app) can use MCP servers to reach tools and data beyond your repository. You add one either with a single codex mcp add command or by editing config.toml , and all Codex surfaces share the same configuration. This guide covers both, with examples built from OpenAI's documentation. Quick answer Run codex mcp add <name> -- <command> <args> . For example codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp (the example OpenAI's docs use). Run codex mcp list to confirm it is saved. Start codex and type /mcp to see the active servers. The command writes a [mcp_servers.<name>] table into ~/.codex/config.toml . You can edit that file directly for anything the command does not cover. The IDE extension and desktop app also have an MCP servers screen (in settings) that edits the same configuration. Where the config lives Global: ~/.codex/config.toml (on Windows, in .codex under your user folder). Project: .codex/config.toml in a project, which Codex reads for trusted projects only. The ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI and the IDE extension share this configuration, so you set a server up once. ChatGPT on the web does not read your local Codex files; it uses plugins instead. Option 1: codex mcp add The general form from OpenAI's docs codex mcp add < server-name > --env VAR1 = VALUE1 --env VAR2 = VALUE2 -- < stdio server-command > Everything after -- is the command that starts the server. Put --env options before it. A few real examples, using servers listed on PluginStack: # Context7: current library docs (example from the OpenAI docs) codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp # Official Memory server codex mcp add memory -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory # Official Filesystem server: the last argument is the folder it may access codex mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem $HOME /projects See Context7 , Memory and Filesystem . The official TypeScript servers need Node 24 or newer from v2 onward ( what changed ). Other commands codex mcp list shows the configured servers. codex mcp --help lists all MCP commands. codex mcp login <server-name> starts the OAuth login for a server that supports it. A remote (HTTP) server For a hosted server, pass its address with --url instead of a command: Then run: codex mcp login example (if the server uses OAuth) codex mcp add example --url https://mcp.example.com Option 2: edit config.toml Each server is a [mcp_servers.<name>] table. For a local (stdio) server, command is required; args , env , env_vars and cwd are optional: ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.filesystem] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "<absolute-path-to-your-projects>"] [mcp_servers.context7] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "@upstash/context7-mcp"] startup_timeout_sec = 20 # default is 10 The table name ( filesystem ) is the label you choose. Save the file and restart Codex (in the IDE extension, use Restart extension ). Environment variables and API keys env sets values for the server: env = { API_KEY = "value" } . env_vars lists variable names to allow and forward from your own environment, such as env_vars = ["API_KEY"] , so the secret does not have to sit in the file. Prefer env_vars for real keys, and never commit a config.toml that contains one. A project-level .codex/config.toml is easy to commit by accident. A remote server in config.toml [mcp_servers.example] url = "https://mcp.example.com" bearer_token_env_var = "EXAMPLE_TOKEN" # token read from this variable, sent in Authorization For HTTP servers, url is required. You can add a bearer token from an environment variable ( bearer_token_env_var ), static headers ( http_headers ), or headers read from variables ( env_http_headers ). With none of those, Codex tries stored OAuth credentials, so run codex mcp login <name> for servers that use OAuth. Useful options startup_timeout_sec : seconds to wait for the server to start. Default 10. Raise it if the first npx download is slow. tool_timeout_sec : seconds a tool call may run. Default 60. enabled = false : switch a server off without deleting its config. required = true : make Codex fail at startup if that server cannot initialise. enabled_tools and disabled_tools : allow or deny specific tool names. default_tools_approval_mode : how Codex asks before running the server's tools ( auto , prompt , writes or approve ). OpenAI's configuration reference has the complete list of MCP options. Settings change between Codex releases, so check it for your version. Check that it works Run codex mcp list : the server should appear. Start codex and type /mcp : the server should be listed as active. Ask for something only that server can do, for example "Use the memory server to remember that I prefer tabs", and approve the tool call if asked. Common errors and fixes The server does not appear: check the table is [mcp_servers.<name>] (plural mcp_servers ) and that the TOML is valid. For a project file, the project must be trusted. It times out on the first run: the first npx -y run downloads the package. Raise startup_timeout_sec , or run the command once by hand so it is cached. spawn npx ENOENT , or it fails only on Windows: update Codex, then see Fix "spawn npx ENOENT" on Windows . The server exits at once: run its command yourself in a terminal to see why. Fix MCP error -32000 walks through it. An OAuth server stays unauthenticated: run codex mcp login <name> ; in the desktop app or IDE extension, use Authenticate in the MCP servers list. Using Codex alongside other tools? The same servers can be added to Cursor and Claude Code . More about the agent itself: Codex CLI . FAQ Is the config the same for the CLI and the IDE extension? Yes. OpenAI's docs say the desktop app, CLI and IDE extension share MCP configuration, so you can switch between them without redoing setup. Where do I put an API key? Use env_vars to forward a variable from your shell, or bearer_token_env_var for remote servers, so the key stays out of the file. If you use env or codex mcp add --env , the value is saved in config.toml ; keep that file private. How do I turn a server off without removing it? Set enabled = false in its [mcp_servers.<name>] table. Sources Commands and config above come from these official docs. Tools change often, so check them for the latest steps. title: Cheapest Object Storage Service for Browser File Uploads: Audit-Controlled Presigned Delivery
summary: A presigned upload is usually the right delivery mechanism for browser receipt ingestion, but the cheapest storage choice is the one that preserves an auditable ownership boundary, not the one with the smallest headline number. For a healthtech system, I would issue a short-lived capability for one immutable object, send the browser directly to object storage, and make the backend verify the resulting object before it enters the receipt ledger. TL;DR: Keep authorization and receipt state in your service; keep byte delivery in object storage. Compare total request, retrieval, retention, and egress behavior for your actual access pattern. A presigned URL reduces delivery work, but it does not prove that a file is valid, complete, or safe to retain. The upload is a capability, not a verdict. The decision record The invariants are narrow and deliberate: A receipt has one server-generated object key, and the key is never derived from an untrusted filename. The upload capability is bound to that key, an expected content type, a size limit enforced by the storage request, and an expiry. The receipt remains pending until a worker checks object metadata, computes a digest, runs malware and format checks, and records an audit event. The original bytes are retained as the evidence object; normalized previews are separate derivatives. That last boundary matters. An HTTP success response proves that a request completed at the transport layer. It does not establish that the payload is the receipt the user intended to submit. Payment and ledger systems teach the same uncomfortable lesson repeatedly: an exactly-once mindset means making state transitions idempotent and observable, not pretending a distributed upload can be exactly once in the physical world. For the browser path, the options look like this: Option Delivery simplicity Access control Audit boundary Appropriate use Backend proxies bytes High for the browser Strong and centralized Easy to correlate Small files or strict network policy Short-lived presigned upload Moderate Strong if the capability is narrow Requires post-upload verification Receipts and other large browser uploads Public or long-lived upload endpoint High initially Weak Difficult to defend Almost never for original records I would choose the middle row for ordinary receipt intake, then spend engineering effort on verification and reconciliation. That is the access-control versus delivery-simplicity trade-off in concrete form. Which object storage service should handle browser file uploads? The reader's word “cheapest” hides several different meters. Stored bytes are only one. A useful estimate includes retained original bytes, metadata and request operations, downloads for human review, failed or repeated uploads, derivative generation, and egress to systems outside the storage region. The correct comparison is a small workload model, not a price-page race. For example, suppose a month contains 80,000 receipts, an average original of 1.8 MB, two review downloads per accepted receipt, and a 30-day retention window before archival policy takes over. Those numbers are planning inputs, not a benchmark. The model should also include a retry factor because mobile browsers disappear between a successful request and the application's final callback. A service with simple delivery but awkward retrieval or lifecycle controls can move cost and operational risk into a later stage. I keep the selection worksheet intentionally boring: region availability, object immutability controls, lifecycle behavior, request granularity, egress semantics, access-log support, and the quality of its S3-compatible or HTTP interface if interoperability is required. The last item is a boundary, not a guarantee; “compatible” still needs tests for multipart behavior, conditional requests, metadata, and error responses. How does the critical path preserve control? The application creates the receipt record before issuing a capability. It never accepts a client-supplied destination, and it does not mark the record complete from a browser callback alone. The following Go sketch shows the shape of that boundary; the storage adapter can target a self-hosted or hosted implementation without changing the receipt state machine. type Receipt struct { \ tID string \ tObjectKey string \ tStatus string \ tDigest string } func StartReceipt ( ctx context . Context , userID string , size int64 , contentType string ) ( Receipt , string , error ) { \ tif size <= 0 || size > 10 << 20 { \ t \ treturn Receipt { } , "" , errors . New ( "receipt size is outside policy" ) \ t } \ tif contentType != "application/pdf" && contentType != "image/jpeg" { \ t \ treturn Receipt { } , "" , errors . New ( "receipt type is outside policy" ) \ t } \ treceipt := Receipt { \ t \ tID : newID ( ) , \ t \ tObjectKey : "receipts/" + newID ( ) , \ t \ tStatus : "pending" , \ t } \ tif err := receiptStore . Insert ( ctx , userID , receipt ) ; err != nil { \ t \ treturn Receipt { } , "" , err \ t } \ turl , err := objectStore . PresignPut ( ctx , receipt . ObjectKey , PresignOptions { \ t \ tContentType : contentType , \ t \ tContentLength : size , \ t \ tExpires : 10 * time . Minute , \ t } ) \ tif err != nil { \ t \ treturn Receipt { } , "" , err \ t } \ treturn receipt , url , nil } The worker then reads the object through a trusted service identity, verifies the observed length and media signature, calculates a digest, and writes an idempotent verification result. If the same event is delivered twice, the receipt ID and object key remain the same, so the second attempt records no second accounting effect. Audit records should include actor, receipt ID, object key, observed metadata, decision, and timestamp; they should not copy the full receipt into every log line. Which failure boundary deserves the most attention? The dangerous gap is between object creation and application state. A user can close the tab after storage accepts the bytes. A callback can be retried. A worker can time out after storing its result but before acknowledging a queue message. None of these conditions justifies deleting the original or promoting it to an accepted receipt without a durable check. A reconciliation job should periodically compare pending records with object metadata, identify orphaned objects under the controlled prefix, and retry verification with an idempotency key. Give unresolved records a quarantine state with an explicit retention rule. This is less glamorous than a fast upload demo, but it is where auditability is won. Caching needs the same restraint. Receipt originals should normally be private and served through an authorization check or a separately issued read capability. Cache-Control is a response policy, not an access-control system; its directives describe caching behavior and must be evaluated alongside the authentication and storage policy. The MDN reference documents that distinction and the available directives. The rejected option, and when it is valid I would reject a backend proxy as the default for larger browser files because every byte consumes application capacity and makes delivery simplicity compete with request handling. It remains valid for small, highly sensitive documents when a network policy requires all bytes to pass through a controlled service, or when the service must transform the stream before storage. That is a different constraint, not evidence that presigned delivery is universally superior. The practical decision rule is therefore modest: choose the storage service whose complete workload model and control surface fit the receipt lifecycle, then isolate it behind a storage interface. Keep the authorization decision, receipt status, verification evidence, and audit trail in your application. The object store should be replaceable infrastructure, while the original receipt and the reasons it was accepted or rejected remain accountable records. References MDN, “Cache-Control header”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control IETF, RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110 IETF, RFC 6749, “The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749

title: An audit report said my site had one schema type. A 25-line script found eight
summary: A third-party audit report landed in my inbox this week. One line said the homepage had "1 valid schema type: Organization". I opened the page source and saw more than that, so I wrote a short script instead of arguing with a PDF. The script It fetches the HTML, pulls out every application/ld+json block, and walks each one, including @graph arrays and nested objects, collecting every @type . import { readFileSync } from "node:fs" ; const src = process . argv [ 2 ] ; const html = src . startsWith ( "http" ) ? await ( await fetch ( src , { headers : { "user-agent" : "Mozilla/5.0" } } ) ) . text ( ) : readFileSync ( src , "utf8" ) ; const blocks = [ . . . html . matchAll ( /< script [ ^> ] + type = [ "']application\/ld\+json[" '][^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/gi)]; const found = []; const walk = (n, block) => { if (Array.isArray(n)) return n.forEach((x) => walk(x, block)); if (n && typeof n === "object") { if (n["@type"]) [].concat(n["@type"]).forEach((t) => found.push({ block, type: t })); Object.values(n).forEach((v) => walk(v, block)); } }; blocks.forEach((m, i) => { try { walk(JSON.parse(m[1]), i); } catch { console.log(`block ${i}: invalid JSON`); } }); console.log(`${blocks.length} JSON-LD blocks`); for (const [t, c] of Object.entries(Object.groupBy(found, (f) => f.type))) console.log(t.padEnd(14), c.length, "in block(s)", [...new Set(c.map((x) => x.block))].join(",")); Object.groupBy needs Node 21 or newer. I ran it on Node v24.18.0. What it printed 4 JSON-LD blocks WebPage 1 in block(s) 0 WebSite 2 in block(s) 0,1 Organization 1 in block(s) 2 ImageObject 1 in block(s) 2 Person 1 in block(s) 2 FAQPage 1 in block(s) 3 Question 5 in block(s) 3 Answer 5 in block(s) 3 Eight distinct types, not one. The count depends on what you call a "type". Four blocks. Eight distinct @type values. Seventeen typed nodes once you count the five questions and five answers. The report's "1" matches none of those. Why a count can differ I do not know why that tool saw one type. Plausible causes, none of them verified: It reads only one block, and the Organization block is the one it kept. It ignores nested nodes, so Person and ImageObject inside the Organization never show up. It validates against a stricter ruleset and silently drops types it does not recognise. The useful part is that all three are cheap to rule out yourself. Run the script on the raw HTML, then on the rendered DOM, and compare. Check the whole site, not one URL A homepage check says nothing about the other pages. I ran the same kind of check through a small crawler over all 152 pages in the sitemap. Every page returned 200, and every page carried JSON-LD. That is a presence check, not a validity check. Caveats Present is not the same as correct. Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema.org validator answer a different question from this script. Google narrowed FAQ rich results in 2023, so I do not expect a visible result from the FAQPage block. It describes the on-page questions, and that is all. I fetched the server HTML. A page that injects JSON-LD with JavaScript needs a rendered-DOM pass too. One audit tool's error says little about other tools. I checked one report. Takeaways When a report quotes a count, reproduce it with a script you can read. Say what you are counting: blocks, distinct types, or typed nodes. Walk @graph and nested objects, or you will undercount. Check presence site-wide, then validity with Google's own tools.
